\chapter{Toward, and What You Have}
\label{ch:mr-kade-and-have}
\hlchaptermodality{48}

\begin{chapteropening}
\textbf{By the end of this chapter:} \emph{I can send somebody left or right, go to somebody's place, and say what I have and do not have in a language that has no verb for having.}

Complete MR-R48-have-and-toward and give a direction, state a possession and hand something over -- ujvīkaḍe jā, mājhyākaḍe pāṇī āhe, mī mitrālā pāṇī deto.
\end{chapteropening}

\section[-kaḍe]{-\mr{कडे} (-kaḍe) — toward, at somebody's side}

\label{lesson:MR-C48-kade}



\begin{quote}
Chapter forty-four gave you \textbf{\mr{उजवा}} and \textbf{\mr{डावा}}, and a warning: naming a side is not the same as sending somebody toward it.

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Recall:} say the two sides, then \emph{mitrālā pāṇī deto}
\end{itemize}
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: -\mr{कडे}}
\begin{quote}
\textbf{-\mr{कडे}} — \emph{-kaḍe} — \textbf{toward; at (somebody's) side}
\end{quote}

\begin{quote}
\textbf{\mr{उजवीकडे} \mr{जा}.} — \emph{ujvīkaḍe jā.} — \textbf{go to the right.}
\end{quote}

\begin{quote}
\textbf{\mr{डावीकडे}} — \emph{ḍāvīkaḍe} — \textbf{to the left.}
\end{quote}

That is a direction rather than a description, and it is the reason chapter forty-four ended where it did. \textbf{-\mr{कडे}} goes on the \textbf{feminine} form — \textbf{\mr{उजवी}}, \textbf{\mr{डावी}} — because the noun it agrees with, \emph{\mr{बाजू}} (side), is feminine even when nobody says it.

It works on people too: \textbf{\mr{मित्राकडे}} is \emph{toward my friend}, or \emph{at my friend's place}. Marathi does not distinguish going to somebody and going to where they are; the side of a person and their house are the same idea.

\begin{quote}
\textbf{\mr{मी} \mr{मित्राकडे} \mr{जातो}.} — \emph{mī mitrākaḍe jāto.} — \textbf{I go to my friend's.}
\end{quote}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{ujvīkaḍe}, \emph{ḍāvīkaḍe} — right, left
  \item \emph{mī mitrākaḍe jāto}
  \item \emph{kuṭhūn} and then \emph{kuṭhe} — where from, and where to
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Which form of \textbf{\mr{उजवा}} does \textbf{-\mr{कडे}} attach to, and why? (\textbf{\mr{उजवी}} — the unspoken noun \emph{side} is feminine.) What does \textbf{\mr{मित्राकडे}} mean besides \emph{toward my friend}? (\textbf{At my friend's place}.)

Sources: \href{https://en.wiktionary.org/wiki/\%E0\%A4\%95\%E0\%A4\%A1\%E0\%A5\%87}{Wiktionary: \mr{कडे}}.
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[mājhyākaḍe … āhe]{\mr{माझ्याकडे} … \mr{आहे} — the sentence Marathi uses instead of \textquotedblleft{}have\textquotedblright{}}

\label{lesson:MR-C48-possession}



\begin{quote}
Look for a Marathi verb meaning \emph{to have} and you will not find one. Forty-eight chapters in, this book has never taught it, and the reason is that it does not exist.
\end{quote}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={Grammar Lens: possession is a place, not an action}]
\begin{quote}
\textbf{\mr{माझ्याकडे} \mr{पाणी} \mr{आहे}.} — \emph{mājhyākaḍe pāṇī āhe.} — \textbf{I have water.}
\end{quote}

Word for word that is \emph{at-my-side water is}. Marathi says having by saying \textbf{where the thing is}, and the whole construction is made of pieces you already own: a pronoun through its possessive oblique, the \textbf{-\mr{कडे}} of one lesson ago, and \textbf{\mr{आहे}}.

Two things follow, and both are worth noticing now rather than discovering later.

The thing possessed is the SUBJECT, so \textbf{\mr{आहे}} agrees with it and not with you. And to deny it you negate that same verb, exactly as chapter thirty-two taught:

\begin{quote}
\textbf{\mr{माझ्याकडे} \mr{पाणी} \mr{नाही}.} — \emph{mājhyākaḍe pāṇī nāhī.} — \textbf{I don't have water.}
\end{quote}

Swap the person and nothing else changes: \textbf{\mr{मित्राकडे} \mr{पाणी} \mr{आहे}}, \emph{my friend has water}.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Say it:} \emph{mājhyākaḍe pāṇī āhe}
  \item \emph{Say it:} \emph{mājhyākaḍe pāṇī nāhī}
  \item \emph{Say it:} \emph{mitrākaḍe pāṇī āhe}
  \item \emph{Recall:} say \textbf{\mr{बसणे}} and then invite somebody to sit — \emph{khālī basā}
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Which word in \textbf{\mr{माझ्याकडे} \mr{पाणी} \mr{आहे}} is the subject? (\textbf{\mr{पाणी}} — the thing, not the owner.) How do you say you do NOT have it? (\textbf{Negate \mr{आहे}: \mr{नाही}}.)
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[-kaḍe]{Send somebody, and say what you have}

\label{lesson:MR-R48-have-and-toward}



\begin{quote}
\textbf{-\mr{कडे}} did three jobs in two lessons. Name them.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{Your turn}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Say it:} \emph{ujvīkaḍe}, \emph{ḍāvīkaḍe} — a direction
  \item \emph{Say it:} \emph{mitrākaḍe} — at his place
  \item \emph{Say it:} \emph{mājhyākaḍe pāṇī āhe} — the whole of \emph{have}
  \item \emph{Say it:} answer \emph{kuṭhe?} with \emph{gharāsamor} and \emph{gharājavaḷ}
  \item \emph{Recall:} say \textbf{\mr{वाटणे}} and how it puts the feeler in the dative
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Marathi has no verb \emph{to have}. What does it use instead? (\textbf{-\mr{कडे} plus \mr{आहे}} — the thing is at your side.) Which ending marks the person a thing is given TO? (\textbf{-\mr{ला}}.) Then stop.
\end{tcolorbox}
